questions.q: Why is an image tag like myapp:1.4.2 described as a 'mutable pointer' rather than a true version?
options: Tags are cryptographically signed and can never be changed once pushed
A later docker push using the exact same tag name silently repoints that tag to a different image in the registry
Tags are only labels used by Docker Hub's web UI with no effect on docker pull
Tag names are case-sensitive and nothing else distinguishes them from a version
questions.explain: A tag is just a label in the registry; pushing again with the same tag name moves that label to point at the new image, so the tag itself offers no guarantee of immutability.

questions.q: Why is deploying from myapp:latest in production considered risky?
options: latest is a floating tag that changes with every push, so two pulls at different times can silently return different code with no warning
The latest tag is deprecated and Docker no longer supports it
latest images are always larger in size than versioned images
latest can only be pulled from Docker Hub, never from ACR or ECR
questions.explain: latest simply means 'whatever was pushed most recently' — it moves forward with every push, so it can't tell you, or a cluster, exactly what code is running.

questions.q: In the scheme docker tag myapp:1.4.2 myapp:1.4 and myapp:1, what are the 1.4 and 1 tags for?
options: They are required by Docker and have no independent meaning
They mark the image as deprecated
Floating convenience tags intentionally moved forward across releases, giving consumers automatic minor/patch updates if they track them
They indicate the image failed its vulnerability scan
questions.explain: 1.4 and 1 are floating tags deliberately re-pointed with each new patch/minor release, alongside the fully pinned 1.4.2, so different consumers can choose their own update cadence.

questions.q: What does pulling an image by its digest (myapp@sha256:...) guarantee that pulling by tag does not?
options: Faster download speed than any tag-based pull
That the registry will automatically scan the image for vulnerabilities on every pull
Automatic compatibility with any CPU architecture
That you get exactly the same bytes every time, since the digest is a content-addressed hash of the image manifest that cannot be repointed
questions.explain: A digest is a SHA-256 hash of the manifest itself; unlike a tag, it cannot be moved to point at different content, so it's the one reference guaranteed to always resolve to the same bytes.

questions.q: How does authenticating docker push to Amazon ECR differ from pushing to Docker Hub, per this lesson's example?
options: ECR requires a short-lived token obtained via the AWS CLI (aws ecr get-login-password), piped into docker login, rather than a Docker Hub account/password
ECR pushes never require any authentication at all
ECR images must be pushed using the az CLI instead of the aws CLI
ECR does not support image tags, only digests
questions.explain: aws ecr get-login-password returns a short-lived token from the already-authenticated AWS CLI session, piped into docker login, instead of a long-lived Docker Hub username/password.
